newsitem.title: USA: Bonds rally as investors bet on "split" election.
newsitem.headline: Bonds rally as investors bet on "split" election.

text.p: Bonds rallied Tuesday as investors bet President Clinton would win re-election and Republicans would keep control of the House, pointing to more modest economic growth and low inflation ahead.

The gains extended a rally that started in earnest last week after reports showed economic growth slowed in the third quarter from a burst of growth last spring. The reports also pointed to minimal inflationary pressures in the economy.

Tuesday's rally drove long-term interest rates to their lowest level in more than seven months as investors said the market appeared ready to absorb $18.5 billion of new three-year notes to be auctioned later in the day, the first leg of the Treasury's quarterly auction.

"The market is getting some support from the sense that the election is going to produce a divided government," said James Glassman, senior economist at Chase Securities Inc. Recent polls showed the Republicans "have a better chance of hanging on to control of the House," he added.
The split means the two parties would check each other's economic policies and keep growth moderate without producing a burst of inflation, which erodes the returns on a bond investor's money.
Analysts said a Republican-led Congress also would bolster chances for a balanced federal budget in coming years, something many on Wall Street would like to see.
The 30-year Treasury bnod rose 29/32, or $9.06 on a $1,000 bond, lowering its yield, which moves in the opposite direction from the price, to 6.59 percent from 6.66 percent late on Monday.

The rate on the 30-year bond has now fallen about a quarter point since late last month, which could lead to lower payments for millions of Americans on mortgages and other loans, many of them tied to long-term bond market rates.
The rally spilled over into the stock market, where the Dow Jones industrial average rose 43.60 points to 6,085.28 at midday.
Strong demand from overseas, notably from Asia and several foreign central banks, also fuelled the bond rally, investors and market analysts said.
"Talk of foreigners buying heavily was all over the place," said one trader at a U.S. investment bank.
Investors appeared confident heading into the auction of three-year notes on Tuesday. The $18.5 billion sale is the first leg of the Treasury's quarterly auction.

The Treasury plans to sell $10 billion of 10-year notes on Wednesday and $10 billion of 30-year bonds on Thursday. The funds are used to repay investors whose bonds are maturing and to fund government operations.
